# The Personal Computer and the New Consumer Monopoly {#sec-4-09}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1975–1985
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What happens when computing reaches the masses?

**The answer.** The chokepoint moves up a layer. When computing reached
individuals the hardware commoditised almost immediately — and the money went to
whoever controlled the layer above it. Microsoft licensed an operating system to
IBM while retaining the right to license it to everyone else, and that single
contractual reservation was worth more than any factory in the industry.

**The mechanism.** Chokepoint control, relocated. The chapter's argument is that
platform control is the same manoeuvre as Act II ch. 10's move into legal
doctrine: get out of the visible, capital-intensive, competable layer, and into
the invisible one that everything must route through.

**The key fact.** The 1980 IBM agreement was non-exclusive. IBM, the most
powerful computer company in the world, did not insist on exclusivity for the
operating system of its personal computer, and that omission created the
industry's dominant firm.

**The human anchor.** The Xerox PARC demonstration in December 1979, and Steve
Jobs walking out of a building where a corporation had already invented the
future and could not work out what to do with it.

**Excluded voices.** The hardware assembly workforce, increasingly offshore, and
the homebrew culture whose free exchange of designs was enclosed within a few
years — including the open letter about hobbyist copying that announced the
enclosure.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that platform control supersedes hardware by
showing an industry in which the hardware makers competed their margins away
while the operating system licensor took the surplus.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** A non-exclusive clause. The most valuable sentence in the history
   of software, and IBM agreed to it.
2. **The Homebrew Computer Club.** Free circulation of designs, 1975. Establish
   what was normal before it stopped being normal.
3. **Apple, 1976.** Wozniak's engineering and Jobs's positioning. The Apple II
   as the first machine sold as a product rather than a kit.
4. **PARC, December 1979.** What Xerox had — the graphical interface, the mouse,
   networking — and the structural reason a copier company could not
   commercialise it.
5. **IBM enters, 1981.** Open architecture, off-the-shelf parts, and the clone
   industry that follows. Hardware commoditises.
6. **The MS-DOS deal.** The specific terms, the non-exclusivity, and how it
   converted into Windows dominance. Follow the contract, not the personalities.
7. **Bayh-Dole, 1980, noted.** One sentence; ch. 10 does the work.
8. **Where the money ended up.** Sourced margins: assemblers against the
   operating system licensor. The arithmetic is the argument.
9. **The excluded.** Offshore assembly; the enclosure of the hobbyist commons.
10. **Landing.** The lesson relearned every twenty years in this book: never own
   the layer that can be competed. Own the one everything passes through.
:::
